title: Floating point: why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why floating point loses precision, compare values correctly, and recognise the situations where you should not be using it at all.

blocks.caption: The demonstration everyone should run once

blocks.text: This is not a bug in C, in your compiler, or in your machine. It is the same in every language that uses the same hardware representation, and the reason is simple: 0.1 cannot be written exactly in binary, any more than one third can be written exactly in decimal.

blocks.title: Never compare floating point with ==
blocks.text: Two computations that should give the same answer often differ in the last bits, so equality fails for values that are equal in every sense that matters. Compare against a tolerance instead — and choose the tolerance deliberately, because a fixed epsilon that works for values near 1 is meaningless for values near a million.

blocks.title: NaN is not equal to itself, and that is deliberate
blocks.text: It means x != x is a valid NaN test, and it means a NaN silently poisons every calculation it touches — every comparison involving it is false, including >= and <=. When a result becomes NaN, look for a division by zero, a square root of a negative, or a parse that produced nothing.
Where floating point is the wrong tool

items: Money — store minor units as integers; a fraction of a cent that rounds the wrong way is a real defect
Counters and identifiers — an integer that must be exact should be an integer
Accumulating many small values — error compounds, so sum in a wider type or use a compensated sum
Equality-driven logic — if the correctness of the program depends on two values being exactly equal, floating point is the wrong representation

blocks.caption: Precision is a display choice, not a value change
lines: printf("%f\n",    x);    /* 0.300000 — six digits by default, which HIDES the problem */
printf("%.20f\n", x);    /* 0.30000000000000004441 — the actual stored value */

blocks.title: The default six digits is why this surprises people
blocks.text: printf("%f") rounds to six decimal places, so a value that is wrong in the seventeenth digit prints as if it were exact. When you are investigating a floating-point discrepancy, print with %.20f or %a — otherwise the output agrees with your expectation and the bug stays hidden.

blocks.expected: A value that is not what it printed, exact and inexact fractions side by side, a money calculation that drifts and an integer one that does not, and NaN failing to equal itself. Running this once removes most future confusion about floating point.

cheatsheet: Only fractions with power-of-two denominators are exact in binary
0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in every language using the same hardware format
Never compare floats with == ; compare against a tolerance
Absolute tolerance for known small scales; relative tolerance for large values
float is about 7 significant digits, double about 15-16
NaN is not equal to itself; test with isnan, not ==
Any comparison involving NaN is false, including >= and <=
Money belongs in integer minor units, not in floating point
printf("%f") shows six digits and hides the problem; use %.20f or %a to investigate

choices.B: 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly in binary, so the stored values are slightly off before the addition happens
choices.D: double is too small for these values

checkpoint.explanation: Only fractions whose denominator is a power of two are exact. This is a property of the representation, identical in every language using the same hardware format.

checkpoint.prompt: How should two floating-point values be compared?

choices.B: By checking that the difference is within a tolerance chosen for the scale of the values
choices.D: By printing both and comparing the strings

checkpoint.explanation: A fixed epsilon that works near 1 is meaningless near a million, which is why a relative tolerance is usually the right choice.

checkpoint.prompt: Why should money not be stored in a double?

choices.B: Repeated addition accumulates error, so totals drift — store minor units as integers instead
choices.C: double cannot represent decimals at all
choices.D: It is slower than integer arithmetic

checkpoint.explanation: Adding 0.01 a thousand times does not give exactly 10. Integer cents are exact, and rounding then happens only where you decide it should.

checkpoint.prompt: How do you test whether a value is NaN?

choices.B: isnan(x) from <math.h> — NaN is not equal to anything, including itself

checkpoint.explanation: Every comparison involving NaN is false, so == can never detect it. That property also means x != x works as a test, but isnan states the intent.
